documents.title: Generative AI (guidance incl. 'Adhere to the Academic Policy')
documents.summary: OIT's institute-wide generative AI page encourages thoughtful use of GenAI and lists security, privacy, legal, copyright and integrity considerations. For academic use it defers to College and School policies and tells faculty to state acceptable use to students and students to ask instructors; the remainder covers phishing, reviewing AI content before publishing, protecting confidential data, and OIT review of AI tool purchases.

units.anchor: category of AI capable of analyzing and emulating datasets to generate various forms of content
units.policy: Generative AI is defined as a category of AI that analyzes and emulates datasets to generate content such as text, images, music, video and code in response to inputs.

units.anchor: Georgia Tech encourages the thoughtful use of Gen AI technologies such as Chat GPT
emphasizing the need for mindful engagement with these tools
units.policy: Use of GenAI tools requires mindful engagement.

units.anchor: safeguarding information security and data privacy
units.policy: Safeguarding information security and data privacy is a key aspect to consider when using GenAI tools.

units.anchor: adhering to legal and regulatory standards, respecting copyright laws
units.policy: Adhering to legal and regulatory standards and respecting copyright law are key aspects to consider when using GenAI tools.

units.anchor: maintaining academic honesty and integrity
units.policy: Maintaining academic honesty and integrity is a key aspect to consider when using GenAI tools.

units.anchor: Gen AI assists in coding, by suggesting code snippets, debugging, or even writing simple programs.
It's used to create educational content, like interactive learning modules
units.policy: GenAI is used to create educational content such as interactive learning modules and to personalize learning based on student performance.

units.anchor: Examine the handbooks and policies of your respective College and School
units.policy: Students and faculty should examine their College's and School's handbooks and policies on generative AI, particularly those pertaining to students and faculty.

units.anchor: Schools will revise and formulate new policies
units.policy: As understanding of generative AI's impacts grows, Schools are anticipated to revise and formulate new policies.

units.anchor: Faculty members should, in the interim, communicate explicitly to their students about the acceptable use
units.policy: Faculty should, in the interim, communicate explicitly to students about acceptable use of generative AI in classes and academic projects.

units.anchor: Students should also proactively seek clarification from their instructors regarding these policies as required.
simplified the process for malevolent individuals to craft advanced phishing emails and produce "deepfakes"
units.policy: Generative AI makes it easier for malicious actors to craft advanced phishing emails and produce deepfakes at scale.

units.anchor: Content created by AI can sometimes be incorrect, deceptive, or entirely made up
it might also include material that is protected by copyright
units.policy: AI-created content might include material protected by copyright.

units.anchor: When you publish anything that incorporates material generated by AI, you bear responsibility
units.policy: Whoever publishes anything that incorporates AI-generated material bears responsibility for that content.

units.anchor: You should not input data categorized as PII
units.policy: Data categorized as PII (including non-public research data, financial, HR, student records and medical information) should not be input into publicly accessible generative AI tools, per Georgia Tech's Information Security Policy.

units.anchor: Information disclosed to Generative AI tools under standard settings is not confidential
should only be used with Generative AI tools that have undergone evaluation and received approval
units.policy: Data at Level 2 or higher in confidentiality should only be used with generative AI tools evaluated and approved by Georgia Tech's Information Security and Data Privacy office.

units.anchor: Connect with OIT before purchasing any generative AI tools
As OIT explores introducing its own Gen AI service offerings
units.policy: OIT is exploring introducing its own GenAI service offerings and works to ensure acquired tools have suitable privacy and security measures.

units.anchor: It is imperative for vendor-supplied generative AI tools to undergo a risk evaluation by OIT
units.frag_end: before they are put to use.
units.policy: Vendor-supplied generative AI tools must undergo a risk evaluation by OIT before they are put to use.

documents.title: Establishing Course Policies (Student Use of Artificial Intelligence section)
documents.summary: CTL's page on establishing course policies includes a 'Student Use of Artificial Intelligence' section telling instructors to state in the syllabus how students may collaborate with and cite GenAI, explaining why silence causes misuse or overcaution, and recommending treating GenAI as an extension of collaboration and honesty policies. It points to example and adaptable syllabus statements and poses design questions on permitted collaboration, assignment-level variation, process documentation and citation style; the rest of the page covers non-AI course policies.

units.policy: Instructors should let students know their expectations for how students should collaborate with and cite their use of GenAI platforms.

units.policy: Microsoft Copilot and other approved systems are named as the GenAI platforms students use.

units.policy: Without AI expectations in the syllabus, students will not know how they can ethically use GenAI in the course.

units.anchor: This misunderstanding can lead students to use GenAI in ways you do not intend.
they may overuse GenAI when you intend for them to complete work independently
units.policy: Without a clear syllabus policy, students may overuse GenAI when the instructor intends independent work.

units.anchor: they may resist using basic GenAI functions such as spelling and grammar assistants
units.policy: Without a clear syllabus policy, students may avoid basic GenAI functions such as spelling and grammar assistants for fear of penalization.

units.anchor: consider students' engagement with GenAI as an extension of your collaboration and academic honesty policies
units.policy: The best way for instructors to develop an AI policy is to treat students' engagement with GenAI as an extension of their collaboration and academic honesty policies.

units.policy: Instructors creating a GenAI usage policy may explore a curated document of cross-institutional example syllabus statements on GenAI use.

units.policy: Instructors should decide how GenAI applications are to appear in citations (e.g., APA, Chicago, MLA).

documents.summary: CS 2050 treats AI assistance like collaboration with people: students may discuss ideas and work with AI, but everything submitted must be written directly by the student, and including anything else is academic misconduct. Two heuristics (never copy from the AI conversation; never have the assignment and AI open together, including AI built into the composition environment) are offered as a safe line, and an integrity policy lets staff ask students to explain submissions, with unexplained work invalidated.

documents.title: ECE 2035 Programming HW/SW Systems Syllabus, Section B, Fall 2026 (Collaboration, Group Work, and Use of Generative AI)
documents.summary: ECE 2035 Section B covers AI in its academic integrity rule: students must not accept, copy or solicit code from, share code with, debug code with, or discuss code performance with any AI assistant or any person other than instructors and TAs. The syllabus's generative AI section simply points back to this 'AI assistant or any person' wording, and exams ban outside resources and any other program or website.

units.anchor: must not accept/copy/solicit code from
units.policy: Students must not accept, copy or solicit code from any AI assistant or any person except the instructors and TAs.

units.anchor: share code with
units.policy: Students must not share code with any AI assistant or any person except the instructors and TAs.

units.anchor: debug code, or discuss its performance with any AI assistant or any person
units.policy: Students must not debug code, or discuss its performance, with any AI assistant or any person except the instructors and TAs.

units.anchor: note the reference to "AI assistant or any person."
units.policy: The course's rule on collaboration and generative AI is the Academic Integrity section, which applies the same limits to AI assistants as to any person.

units.anchor: use of any other program or web site is prohibited
units.frag_end: program or web site is prohibited.
units.policy: During exams, use of outside resources, phones, communication between students, and any other program or website is prohibited.

notes: Coder B dry run. CS 6750, CS 7637 and CSE 6040 share the same OMSCS AI Collaboration Policy text and were each coded in full. The CS 2050 permission to copy one's own work into the AI conversation was coded as P20 with modality 'may' (the converse of the P20 prohibition).
